sense: how far something goes; the degree

terms.grammar: adverb, in indirect questions; answered by eātenus, “so far”
evidence: Cic. Lael. 61: est enim quātenus amīcitiae darī venia possit
Cic. de Or. 2.237: quātenus sint rīdicula tractanda ōrātōrī (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Properly “up to where”. The answer is eātenus, “so far, to that extent”, with quoad or ut (Cic. Leg. 1.14, Lewis & Short). In Horace and later, quātenus also means “since, seeing that” (Lewis & Short).

terms.gloss: to such an extent that, so … that
evidence: Hor. Ep. 1.1.39: nēmō adeō ferus est, ut nōn mītēscere possit
Cic. Fl. 47: nēminem quidem adeō īnfatuāre potuit, ut eī nummum ūllum crēderet (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: With verbs, adjectives and nouns, in every period (Lewis & Short); ūsque adeō is stronger, “so very much”.

terms.gloss: to some extent, in some measure
evidence: Sen. Ep. 116.3: aliquātenus, inquis, dolēre, aliquātenus timēre permitte
terms.comment: Post-Augustan (Seneca, Quintilian, Pliny), as Lewis & Short marks it.

phrases.latin: est enim quātenus amīcitiae darī venia possit
phrases.english: for there is a point up to which friendship may be indulged

phrases.latin: nēmō adeō ferus est, ut nōn mītēscere possit, sī modo cultūrae patientem commodet aurem
phrases.english: no one is so wild that he cannot be tamed, if only he lends a patient ear to training

phrases.latin: Aliquātenus, inquis, dolēre, aliquātenus timēre permitte
phrases.english: “Allow me to grieve to some extent,” you say, “and to fear to some extent”

seneca-section.html: Lewis & Short cites the passage as Sen. Ep. 116, 4; in the Perseus text it stands in section 3, which we follow.
